item.title: Did 75,000 Students Cheat on a College-Entrance Exam in Mexico?
item.description: The country’s largest public university is requiring all students who passed its entrance exam to take a new test after experts found evidence of widespread cheating, including with A.I.
item.dc:creator: Annie Correal
item.media:description: The National Autonomous University of Mexico, UNAM, in Mexico City.

item.title: Trump Administration Plans to Upend Head Start by Deregulating It
item.description: The White House tried but failed to block funding for preschool for poor children. Instead, it will seek to strip away standards on health, literacy — and brushing teeth.
item.dc:creator: Coral Davenport
item.media:description: A teacher at a Head Start program run by Easterseals South Florida instructing students on reading and writing. Head Start has served over 30 million children since it was created.

item.title: You’re Welcome at SUNY, New York Tells Students Disenrolled by Howard
item.description: The Washington, D.C., university told incoming freshmen who missed a tuition deadline that they no longer had a spot. But they now can attend a New York State school or CUNY.
item.dc:creator: Caitlyn Freeman
item.category: State University of New York at Albany
State University of New York at Buffalo
State University of New York at Stony Brook
item.media:credit: Johnny Milano for The New York Times
item.media:description: The State University of New York at Stony Brook is among the SUNY campuses accepting students disenrolled by Howard University.

item.title: Mildred Pitts Walter, Author of Books for Black Children, Dies at 103
item.description: Teaching kindergarten in South Central Los Angeles in the 1950s and ’60s, she realized that her students were not represented in the books they read. So she wrote her own.
item.dc:creator: Richard Sandomir
item.media:description: Mildred Pitts Walter in 1971. Over three decades, she wrote more than 20 books that “changed the course of children’s literature,” said Lin Oliver, a founder of the Society of Children’s Book Writers and Illustrators.

item.title: Texas Parents Try New Tactic to Remove Ten Commandments From Schools
item.description: A lawsuit filed by three parents argues that the displays violate a state religious freedom law and asks for them to be removed before school starts in August.
item.dc:creator: J. David Goodman
item.media:credit: Desiree Rios for The New York Times
item.media:description: A Ten Commandments poster displayed in a classroom in Fort Worth, Texas.

item.title: Florida Professor Fired for Assigning a Profane Story, Lawsuit Says
item.description: South Florida State College fired an English professor after she assigned a story about a teacher who talks about sex with her students. Now the professor is suing.
item.dc:creator: David Ovalle
item.category: Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (Nonprofit)
item.media:credit: Jacob Langston for The New York Times
item.media:description: Vinita Prabhakar, who taught English at South Florida State College, said in an interview that she assigned the story to challenge her students.

item.title: Conservatives Like the Liberal Arts, Actually. They Just Don’t Like the Phrase.
item.description: Some people revere the “liberal arts” while others call them useless. They’re probably talking about different things.
item.dc:creator: Nitsuh Abebe

item.title: To Recruit Teachers, School Districts Are Building Homes
item.description: The nation’s housing shortage has made it challenging for some essential workers like educators to live where they work. An increasing number of school districts are trying to change that.
item.dc:creator: Patrick Sisson
item.media:credit: Ariana Drehsler for The New York Times
item.media:description: School districts are actively pursuing developers to turn their excess land and underutilized buildings into housing. LIVIA Scripps Ranch, a 264-unit multifamily complex in California, is on a former school site.

item.title: Investigation of School Epstein Helped Finds Abuses Went Beyond Him
item.description: A law firm hired by Interlochen, the arts school and camp, to look into alumni complaints of sexual abuse fielded dozens of disturbing accounts, primarily from decades ago.
item.dc:creator: Graham Bowley
item.media:credit: Jamie Kelter Davis for The New York Times
item.media:description: After a complaint from an alumnus, Interlochen hired a law firm to investigate allegations that teachers and other staff at the Michigan school had acted inappropriately, and worse, with students.

item.title: ‘We Are Not Learning Anything’: India’s Gen Z Rage Is a Test for Modi
item.description: As India’s huge youth population surges, the government faces pressure to fix an education system that leaves many ill prepared for university, let alone for the workplace.
item.dc:creator: Pragati K.B. and Somini Sengupta
item.media:credit: Saumya Khandelwal for The New York Times
item.media:description: Protesters demanding the resignation of India’s education minister last week.

item.title: Secret Service Agent and 2 Others Charged in Near-Fatal Fraternity Hazing
item.description: A college fraternity member was paddled so severely during hazing rituals that he suffered kidney damage and nearly died.
item.dc:creator: David Ovalle
item.media:description: According to an arrest warrant, investigators identified the victim as a law student at the University of Miami and the fraternity involved as Kappa Alpha Psi, which officially prohibits hazing.

item.title: Cornell, Northwestern and Other Universities Plan for Classes at Middle East Campuses
item.description: Even after the collapse of the cease-fire between the United States and Iran, American universities expect to teach in Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, and a new outpost is on track to open in Saudi Arabia.
item.dc:creator: Alan Blinder
item.category: US and Israeli Attack on Iran (2026)
item.media:credit: Bernd von Jutrczenka/Picture-Alliance/DPA, via Associated Press Images
item.media:description: The University of New Haven is still planning to inaugurate its new campus in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

item.title: India’s Education Minister Steps Down in Victory for Cockroach Party Protesters
item.description: The Cockroach Janta Party called an end to weeks of protests after the education minister resigned, a win for that movement even as deep-seated anger among young people remains.
item.dc:creator: Anupreeta Das and Showkat Nanda
item.media:credit: Saumya Khandelwal for The New York Times
item.media:description: Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party, in New Delhi on Saturday celebrating the resignation of India’s education minister.

item.title: More Than 500 Howard University Students Are Bumped From Enrollment
item.description: The university said the students failed to meet payment requirements by a July 10 deadline and were removed from the school’s enrollment weeks before they were to move in.
item.dc:creator: Mark Walker and Emmett Lindner
item.media:credit: Maansi Srivastava for The New York Times
item.media:description: Howard is one of the country’s most prestigious historically Black colleges and universities.

item.title: Cambridge Professor’s Jason Arday’s Work Challenged Ahead of Book Launch
item.description: A knife-wielding masked man. A pig’s head outside his parents’ door. Running 30 marathons in 35 days. The Cambridge professor Jason Arday, accused of plagiarism, says he’s been through it all. Not everyone believes him.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Schuessler and Alexandra Alter
item.media:credit: via Simon & Schuster; Photo by Anselm Ebulue

item.title: Education Dept. to Wipe Out Student Loans of 170,000 More Defrauded Borrowers
item.description: The sprawling case, centered on students defrauded by for-profit schools, has now become the largest class-action settlement in American history.
item.dc:creator: Stacy Cowley
item.media:credit: Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group, via Getty Images
item.media:description: Kaplan College was one of the more than 150 institutions, mostly for-profit colleges, named in the 2022 settlement in the case.

item.title: Brown’s President Will Resign after a Tenure that Included Trump Deal
item.description: The president, Christina H. Paxson, led the campus for over a decade, but in recent years faced protests, political pressure and a shooting that killed two students.
item.dc:creator: Alan Blinder
item.media:description: The president of Brown University, Christina H. Paxson, on campus in 2022.

item.title: Another Trump Fiasco: The Reflecting Pool
item.description: Readers see the saga as a symbol of Trump administration failures. Also: Ominous plans for Head Start; land acknowledgments.
item.media:credit: Andrew Leyden for The New York Times
item.media:description: Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney in Washington, concluded that shoddy construction, not vandalism, had caused damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

item.title: Former ’60 Minutes’ Correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi, Scott Pelley Will Teach At Columbia
item.description: Sharyn Alfonsi and Scott Pelley, who exited the show after clashing with executives at CBS News, will teach reporting skills.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Mullin
item.media:credit: From left: Marla Aufmuth/Getty Images; Monica Schipper/Getty Images
item.media:description: Sharyn Alfonsi and Scott Pelley, former “60 Minutes” correspondents, will have part-time roles teaching at Columbia Journalism School.

item.title: After Colleges Reject ‘Compact,’ Trump Officials Try a Letter
item.description: The open letter from Education Secretary Linda McMahon fell far short of the attempt at a compact last year that dangled research money in return for embracing the Trump administration’s agenda.
item.dc:creator: Michael C. Bender and Alan Blinder
item.media:credit: Tierney L. Cross/The New York Times
item.media:description: Linda McMahon, the education secretary, signed the letter that asks every postsecondary institution in the nation to publicly state its commitments and planned changes “before the end of 2026.”
